places.name: Đả Diệp Lâm
places.size: A bamboo forest about 10 km across with a training clearing about 120 m wide holding some 300 cut stumps; no buildings.
places.where: Bamboo forest at 150 m on low hills, inland. Wood qi. No holder; the training ground of Xuyên Lâm Môn's young disciples. Nearest: the village Phạt Trúc 75 km, the village Dẫn Lộ 158 km. Map crop: low green-gold hills thick with bamboo and forest, a river running to a blue bay on the east edge; no mountains close.
places.imagined: A downpour: rain roaring on the leaves like surf, disciples balancing on stumps of different heights.
places.subject: The place: Đả Diệp Lâm, the Forest of Beaten Leaves, seen from above in a downpour. Setting: low green hills covered in dense tall bamboo, so thick that the roof of the grove is a continuous sea of feathery green about ten kilometres across, shaking under heavy rain, with white mist rising from it and streaks of rain visible. In the heart of the grove is a clearing about a hundred and twenty metres wide, filled with the cut stumps of bamboo of different heights, about three hundred, standing in rows like a field of posts, from knee height to head height, each pale gold, cut flat, wet and shining. A dozen young disciples in dark rain cloaks stand and leap on the stumps in a line, practising footwork, tiny figures, with staffs, keeping their balance as the rain hammers the grove. Narrow paths run through the bamboo to the clearing, with a single small thatched shelter at its edge holding staffs. Rain pools silver in hollows. Soft grey-green light from the upper left, wet shine, long shadows. The stumps number three hundred and twelve, cut at heights from the knee to the shoulder in a pattern that rises in long diagonal ranks, and each is about as wide as a man's chest. Four of the stumps in the middle stand taller than the rest, marking the test pillars on which disciples balance on one foot for a full hour. Heavy rain makes the leaves roar, and pale spray rises from the leaves in drifts. A single thatched shed beside the clearing stores two dozen staffs of different lengths, and a bamboo trough collects rainwater from the shed roof.

places.name: Kinh Lôi Mạch
places.size: A spirit vein on a bare black ridge about 5 km long, with seams of violet light and a Thunder Hall and soul-vault entrances of the Tower (about 30 buildings and 100 people).
places.where: High mountain at 3.19 km on Kinh Trập Sơn, within reach of the storm peaks. Metal qi, with Thunder. Held by Thính Vũ Lâu (the Thunder Hall and the soul vaults), 5 tiles from Thiên Xu's border. Nearest: the ruin Nam Vọng Bảo 79 km, the peak Tuyệt Bích Phong 90 km. Map crop: jagged grey and snow-capped crags in every direction, a few small lakes and thin forest in the lower right; no sea or river close.
places.imagined: Thunder rolls and the violet seams in the black rock brighten like veins under skin.
places.subject: The place: Kinh Lôi Mạch, the Vein of Startling Thunder, seen from above a high black ridge. Setting: a bare black ridge of Kinh Trập Sơn at over three kilometres up, with no plant growing on it, snow in the gullies, storm cloud closing around the peaks and a violet-grey sky; the air looks charged. Through the black rock run seams of violet light like veins under skin, hundreds of them, branching and joining along the ridge for five kilometres, each a thin glowing crack from fine as a hair to wide as a road, and at the moment a long thunder rolls the whole network flares brighter, throwing violet glare on the rock. Fused black glass cracks along the seams. On a broad shelf at the heart of the vein stands the Thunder Hall of the sect: a low heavy hall of black stone with a flat roof set with iron lightning rods, about thirty buildings around it, black stone barracks, vault doors cut into the cliff like square mouths with iron gates, a ring of watch-towers, and a paved yard where about a hundred sect cultivators in dark robes stand as tiny figures, watching the sky. A single zigzag stair climbs from the forest far below. Cold violet light with a thin gold gleam from the upper left, long hard shadows. The vein's strongest seam, a violet gash a hundred metres long, runs through the Thunder Hall's own floor and is bridged by a single flagstone causeway. Eight lightning masts rise above the shelf, each hung with copper coils, and their bases are set in pits of fused glass. Soul-vault doors are of black iron, nine of them, each marked with a different glyph-less notch; the largest is guarded by two stone beasts. A watch-bell of bronze hangs on the ridge above and is struck in a long note whenever the lights flare. Sleepers' barracks are half-buried in the rock to resist the strikes.

places.name: Lôi Trạch Thành
places.size: A burned city: once about 16,000 roofs and 70,000 people; ruined walls about 2.4 km across, stones fused black and glassy, now reeds in the streets.
places.where: Temperate forest at sea level on a marshy river mouth by the sea. Wood qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu. Khải Lôi Môn's city built 170, burned by the lightning of Hầu Xuân Lôi's tribulation. Nearest: the forest Hải Trúc Lâm 150 km. Map crop: a river mouth on the western shore of a big blue bay, with marshes and forest around, thick forest to the north-west and a pale ridge of golden hill to the south; faint fields to the south-east.
places.imagined: Grey dawn mist. Broken walls fused black and glassy as if fired in a kiln; the shattered drum tower stump split down its middle.
places.subject: The place: Lôi Trạch Thành, the City of the Thunder Marsh, a burned city, seen from above a marshy river mouth in grey dawn mist. Setting: old forest on the low hills behind, a wide marshy river mouth of reed beds and shallow channels with the grey sea beyond, mist hanging low, a pale sky. The broken walls of a once-great city enclose an area about two and a half kilometres across, in a rough rectangle; the wall stones are fused black and glassy, as if fired in a kiln, shining wet like obsidian, with sagging, melted-looking edges, and gaps where gates stood. Inside, the street grid is still visible as lines of black glassy rubble, with the foundations of thousands of buildings, the rounded fused stumps of walls, a dry harbour with pilings, a broken bridge, and reeds growing through every street in pale green lines. Over the old gate rises the shattered stump of a great drum tower, split down its middle from top to base, the two halves leaning apart, glassy at the break. Black scorch rays radiate across the ground from the tower. Small grey huts of a hamlet of sweepers cluster at one corner, with thin smoke, tiny figures with brooms. Cold pearl light from the upper left, long soft shadows. The fused wall stones fuse into long ribbons that hang from the wall tops like frozen wax. A dry harbour basin about four hundred metres across lies behind the gate, with rotted piles in rows, and a stone breakwater has slumped into the reeds. At the tower's base a drum, as wide as a house, lies cracked on its side, and a circle of nine glassy stumps marks the lost drum court. The sweepers' hamlet has twelve small houses of salvaged black stone, a single shrine and a few sheds, with brooms stacked outside every door, and a path of swept ground that runs a long way into the ruin.

places.name: Thu Phần Các
places.size: A minor sect of soul arts and grave wards: about 35 members, a pavilion with two small towers and about 25 buildings on a hill about 600 m across, slopes covered in hundreds of old grave mounds.
places.where: Bamboo forest at 130 m, a quiet bamboo hill inland, 10 tiles from the ruins of Lôi Trạch Thành. Wood qi. Ma đạo minor sect under Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the lightning wood Kiếp Trúc Lâm 75 km, the village Song Khê 158 km. Map crop: forested bamboo hills with winding rivers, a blue bay of the sea at the east edge, and a thinner grassy coast at the south; no mountains close.
places.imagined: Autumn evening wind: thousands of thin wooden slips brushed with poem lines hanging over graves and clacking softly.
places.subject: The place: Thu Phần Các, the Pavilion of the Autumn Graves, seen from above a quiet bamboo hill at dusk in autumn. Setting: low hills of bamboo in muted green and gold, thin autumn mist in the hollows, a distant glimpse of grey sea. A pavilion of dark weathered wood with two small towers rises on the hill's crown, about twenty-five buildings in all, low, dark-roofed, with long galleries, a courtyard, a kitchen, dormitories for thirty-five, and a drying yard for slips. The slopes below are covered in countless old grave mounds, hundreds of low grassy humps with stone markers and a few sunken tombs, in rows and clusters running down all sides of the hill between the bamboo. Across the graves and between the bamboo stems hang strings of thin wooden slips, thousands, each brushed with a line of an old poem, in long lines stretching from pole to pole, clacking softly in the wind, pale against the dark. A few dozen pale shapes hint at ghosts among the mounds, faint and barely there, and a few figures in dark robes walk the rows copying poem lines onto slips with brushes, tiny. Dim gold light from the upper left, long cool shadows. The pavilion's roof is of dark weathered shingle with upswept corners, and the two small towers carry a bell each. The Sweepers' Lodge is far away at the ruin, so here the disciples are the copyists: a long open copying hall holds twenty desks in rows, each with brush, ink-stone and a pile of blank slips, and drying racks of hung slips fill the courtyard. Each grave mound has a short wooden pole beside it, and the slips on it are tied in sets of nine. A ghost-lantern hangs from every third pole, unlit.

places.name: Phục Hổ Cương
places.size: A long low ridge about 6 km long shaped like a crouching cat; no buildings, the villages far below bar their doors.
places.where: Highland at 1.4 km on the Kinh Trập highland, inland. Metal qi. No holder; a tiger-kind beast's ridge, resource beast bone. Nearest: the peaks Thiên Bộc Phong 160 km, Thùy Liêm Phong 175 km. Map crop: a highland of bare grey and rust-red banded rock ridges with grass only in the hollows, a small lake at the north-west and white crags in the upper half; no sea close.
places.imagined: Spring thunder rolling over the highland, the beasts on the ridge roaring back.
places.subject: The place: Phục Hổ Cương, the Ridge of the Crouching Tiger, seen from above the Kinh Trập highland. Setting: a high highland of bare grey rock ridges banded in rust-red, with tawny grass only in the hollows, with dark thunderclouds gathering on the far peaks and a flash of lightning, long shadows of clouds sliding over the grass. A long, low ridge about six kilometres long lies across the picture, shaped like a great cat crouched with its head on its paws: a rounded head at one end with two small peaks for ears, a long back, a haunch, and a long curved tail. Its exposed rock is banded in yellow and dark grey stripes like a tiger's coat, running across the ridge in bold bars, and the grass on its flanks is flattened into long paths by animals. On the head-hump lies a small flat rock ledge with scattered bones, and a few huge striped beasts, tiger-kin, each as big as a hut, stand and lie on the ridge, tiny against the whole, one with its head raised roaring toward the thunder. Far below, a village's small lights and a herd driven in off the highland, with barred doors. Warm gold light from the upper left breaking through cloud, long shadows. Along the ridge's flanks the ground is scored with a hundred narrow game-paths, and at three spots the stripes of rock form natural dens with clawed entrances, each about the size of a barn door. The tiger-kin's roar can be seen as a ripple of flattened grass running down the slope. Below the ridge the valley farms are small, their walls mended with thorn, and a lone herdsman's hut has its shutters barred. A beacon tower at the highland's edge has a pile of unlit brushwood. Dust blows off the ridge as the thunder comes.

places.name: Lôi Trúc Lâm
places.size: A lightning bamboo wood about 6 km across, with a hermitage of about 20 monks, nuns and novices (about 10 huts) at its edge.
places.where: Bamboo forest at sea level, inland. Wood qi. Held by Cốc Vũ Quán (hermitage since 1180). Nearest: the town Phong Đăng 125 km, the minor seat Cốc Vũ Quán 250 km. Thunder-rooted bamboo. Map crop: a bright green bamboo lowland of forest and meadows with a bay of the sea at the south and the coast at the north-east, a river on the left edge; no mountains.
places.imagined: A hush before thunder: split, charred bamboo poles and fresh shoots, pale glassy sand.
places.subject: The place: Lôi Trúc Lâm, the Thunder Bamboo Wood, seen from above after a storm. Setting: a flat bamboo forest about six kilometres across in a coastal lowland, dark thunderheads clearing to the east, rain shining on the leaves, and a pale sky. The bamboo here is tall and thick, in dense stands, and a large part of it has been struck by lightning: whole groves of poles split lengthwise, charred black on one side with the other side bright green, bursts of scorched bare ground in circular pockets where bolts hit, fused glassy sand shining there in pale pools and branched shapes, and tall poles still smoking faintly. Amid the charred groves, fresh green shoots grow thick from the roots, bright against the black. A narrow path of beaten earth leads in to a hermitage at the edge of the wood: about ten small huts of bamboo and thatch around a courtyard with a tiny shrine with a bell and a well, with a strip of vegetable garden, and about twenty monks, nuns and novices in grey robes cutting fallen poles and tending shoots, tiny figures; a pole is passed to a traveller with a mule. Light from the upper left, long shadows, steam from wet ground. The charred groves are cut off sharply from the unburned ones: a clean line of fresh green meets a belt of black poles. In the strike circles the sand has fused into pale green glass, and in one a bamboo pole lies melted into a twisted rope. The hermitage's huts are about four metres square, on stilts, with a shared kitchen and a bell-frame of three poles. The nuns' garden grows beans and gourds in raised beds. A line of cut poles, seven to a bundle, is stacked beside the path, each marked with a knot of string where a traveller has bought it.

places.name: Cốc Vũ Quán
places.size: A minor sect, a bamboo-hill abbey of about 30 monks, nuns and novices with terrace farmers: a compound about 350 m across with about 30 buildings and farm terraces, founded 610.
places.where: Bamboo forest at 230 m, a bamboo hill above Phong Đăng. Wood qi. Neutral vassal of Thính Vũ Lâu. Nearest: the village Xuân Duẩn 160 km, the village Dẫn Lộ 180 km. Map crop: a green bamboo hill with grassy terraces, a round dense bamboo patch to the north-east, the sea to the east at the edge, and a river to the north-west.
places.imagined: Grain Rain day: monks sowing in rain on terraces under the abbey.
places.subject: The place: Cốc Vũ Quán, the Abbey of Grain Rain, seen from above a bamboo hill in spring rain. Setting: a green bamboo hill above a coastal plain, with a town and a river mouth faint in mist below, and light rain falling. The abbey stands on the hilltop and its shoulder: about thirty buildings of pale timber and grey tile in a walled compound of three courtyards, a main hall with a double-eaved roof, a bell tower, a scripture house, a dozen small cells, a guest house, a bath house, and a granary, with a round gate at the front reached by a long stair of a hundred and eight steps. Below the abbey, farm terraces step down the slope on every side: about forty narrow terraces of rice and millet, sown, with water shining, each held by bamboo-pole walls, with irrigation channels and bamboo pipes. About thirty monks and nuns in grey and ochre robes and novices in straw rain-capes sow and weed the terraces in long lines, tiny figures, and farm families work beside them. A bamboo grove surrounds the whole hill. Soft grey light from the upper left, mist, gentle long shadows. The terraces are of two kinds: wet ones where rice is sown, and dry ones of millet and beans, and the abbey's tiny tea garden grows on the sunniest. The refectory is a long hall with forty places, the scripture house has a roof of green tile, and the hundred and eight steps to the gate are each a different grey stone. Seed-baskets hang at the terrace ends, and a drum is struck to start the sowing. A line of novices carries water in bamboo tubes from the spring.

places.name: Thủ Động Trại
places.size: A ruined mountain fort: walls about 300 m across, once about 40 buildings for a garrison of 200, now broken, with a cave hall in the rock behind it used by the sect's dark singers.
places.where: High mountain at 2.01 km, inland. Metal qi. Holder Thính Vũ Lâu; a former fort. The Cave Hall of Thu Phần Các's dark singers. Nearest: the peak Lôi Trụ Phong 79 km, the peak Vân Hải Đỉnh 112 km. Map crop: rugged grey mountains with rust-orange hills at the upper left and a bay of the sea at the lower-left edge, a dark linear escarpment east of the fort, and thin pockets of forest; no river.
places.imagined: Evening on a high shelf: a broken fort and a cave mouth with a faint pale glow.
places.subject: The place: Thủ Động Trại, the Fort of the Guarding Cave, a ruined fort seen from above a high mountain shelf. Setting: a steep grey mountainside at two thousand metres, pockets of thin pine and snow, scree slopes, a sea of cloud far below in the valleys and blue peaks beyond. A ruined fort stands on a broad shelf: a rough square of broken grey stone wall about three hundred metres across, with towers at the corners, two collapsed, a gate with its timber long gone, and the footings of about forty barracks, stables and storehouses, roofless, with weeds and moss, a dry cistern, and a few fallen beams. Behind the fort a rock cliff rises, and in its foot gapes a tall cave mouth, as wide as a gatehouse, with a worn stone threshold and steps, and a faint pale glow from within. In front of the cave a small level yard has been swept clean, with a row of low stone seats, and a few figures in dark robes sit in a line facing the cave mouth, tiny, the dark singers. Smoke from one small fire. Late gold light from the upper left, long cold shadows. The fort's gate is a stone arch six metres wide, with a collapsed guardroom beside it and a single gate-post still standing. Three of the four corner towers have lost their upper floors, and in the fourth a sapling grows in what was the stair. The cave mouth is nine metres high and ringed with soot; inside, the floor is dressed stone and a hall of tall pillars recedes into the dark, its far end glowing very faintly. The singers' yard is only a hand's breadth cleaner than the fort, and a small fire of juniper smokes there.

places.name: Tử Tinh Khoáng
places.size: A mine on a high shoulder: a pit and about 8 tunnel mouths, about 30 buildings and 250 miners; a Thunder-glass mine of Xuyên Lâm Môn.
places.where: High mountain at 2.38 km, inland. Metal qi (46 %) with Thunder (37 %). Held by Xuyên Lâm Môn; the Tower's thunder-glass. Nearest: the ruin Hắc Phong Trại 90 km, the peak Thiết Trượng Phong 135 km. Map crop: grey rugged mountains with thin forest pockets, a small blue lake to the north-east, rust-orange hills at the far left; no sea or river close.
places.imagined: Crystals of deep purple catching light in the pit walls.
places.subject: The place: Tử Tinh Khoáng, the Purple Crystal Mine, seen from above a high mountain shoulder. Setting: a high stony shoulder at over two thousand metres, thin pines, grey rock and pockets of snow, clouds below and a cold bright sky. An open pit about four hundred metres across is cut into the slope in a stepped bowl of grey rock, its walls glittering with veins and clusters of deep purple crystal, thunder-glass, which glints in the sun; rope hoists and wooden cranes lift baskets of crystals from the pit floor, ore carts run on narrow rails into eight tunnel mouths in the cliff beyond, shored with dark timber, with faint violet light from inside. Spoil fans of purple-grey shards run down the hillside. About thirty buildings of grey stone and slate: a crushing mill with a waterwheel, a sorting hall, miners' barracks, stables for mules, and a store with a locked iron door. About two hundred and fifty miners in wool coats and goggles work the pit and tunnels, tiny figures; a mule train winds down the zigzag road. Cold clear light from the upper left, deep violet shadows in the pit. The pit's crystal veins run in three bands, thick as a man's arm: pale violet, deep purple and nearly black. A rope and pulley rig lowers a cage, and the crushing mill's waterwheel is fed from a mountain tarn by a wooden aqueduct two hundred metres long. In the sorting hall, women in goggles grade the crystals by tint under skylights. The barracks have a double wall against wind, and the locked store is a squat stone vault. A zigzag road with forty-two hairpins descends to the forest, and the chain of mules on it is almost a kilometre long.

places.name: Thần Cổ Phong
places.size: A great sect's new seat on a high peak, taken over 1166-1170: a domain about 5 km across, some 300 members plus servants and mortal families (about 2,000 residents), about 220 buildings; newer, harder halls than the old tower.
places.where: High mountain at 2.8 km, inland on Kinh Trập Sơn. Metal 45 %, Thunder 40. Seat of Thính Vũ Lâu (ma đạo great sect) since the move from the cone. Nearest: the mine Sa Kim Khoáng 79 km, the ruin Thủ Lôi Bảo 79 km. Map crop: rugged grey mountains with thin pockets of forest in the valleys and a dark forested valley to the south-west; no sea or river close.
places.imagined: A storm gathering at dusk: a great drum-shaped hall on the summit, taiko-like drums the size of houses beating thunder answers.
places.subject: The place: Thần Cổ Phong, the Divine Drum Peak, the seat of a great ma đạo sect, seen from above in the dusk of a gathering storm. Setting: a high mountain peak at nearly three kilometres on a thunder range, steep rock slopes of grey and black, snow pockets, bare cliffs with a few twisted pines, a sea of dark cloud below crossed with flickers of lightning, and a violet sky. The peak is shaped like a drum: a broad round summit plateau about a kilometre across with sheer walls, and on it and on terraces down the flanks stands a domain about five kilometres across: about two hundred and twenty buildings in black stone and dark timber with iron-grey roofs, long galleries, gate towers with iron-banded doors, barracks, vault halls cut into rock, training yards of black stone, and switchback roads and stair of a thousand steps from the forest below. On the summit stands a great round drum hall, roofed in a single flattened dome of dark bronze, ringed by twelve smaller drum pavilions, and in the central court a huge drum, thirty metres across, with a drummer's platform, answering the thunder; lightning-rods stand on every roof. Light shows in few windows, and a few thousand people, tiny figures, servants and mortal families, crowd the lower terraces. Dim violet light with a thin gold line from the upper left, long hard shadows. The drum hall's roof is a single flattened bronze dome sixty metres across, green with age, and the twelve smaller pavilions around it each hold a drum the size of a house. Along the summit's walls hang eight hundred iron bells, rung by the wind. Barracks and vault halls are cut into the cliff faces in tiers, and four great stairs, each of a thousand steps, climb the four flanks. Lower down, cultivated terraces of grain and tea supply the servants' quarters, with a market court under a long slate roof. A single bell, cast of captured iron, hangs over the main gate.

places.name: Phần Vũ Đường
places.size: A minor sect of body tempering: about 90 people (30 tempered cultivators, a levy of 50, servants), a hall of red-brown stone in tiers beside a field of about 40 smoking vents; about 40 buildings.
places.where: Grassland at 40 m in the vent country, inland from red cliffs, 5 tiles from the Fire Court. Fire qi. Neutral vassal of Phượng Minh Cung, founded 1020. Nearest: the ruin Hỏa Ti Trấn 125 km, the lava vent Chúc Dung Khẩu 180 km. Map crop: a green and golden neck of land between a gulf on the west and the open sea on the east, with a huge grey-brown volcanic cone just south-west of the place, forest on the cone's east flank, and rolling hills north.
places.imagined: Disciples sitting in the smoking vent pits on worn stone ledges until their feathers burn, and walking out reborn.
places.subject: The place: Phần Vũ Đường, the Hall of Burning Plumes, a small sect of body tempering, seen from above a grassland dotted with smoking vents. Setting: a green and golden neck of land between a gulf on the west and the open sea on the east, the huge grey-brown flank of a volcanic cone rising just to the south-west, and in the grass a field of about forty smoking volcanic vents opening in the ground in pits of various sizes, trailing thin white smoke and shimmering heat, the grass scorched yellow-brown in rings around each. Around the largest vent, about forty metres across, a hall of red-brown stone climbs in tiers, about forty buildings: a main hall with flared tiled roofs, long barracks for the levy, dormitories, a bath house, a store, and a forge, in a walled compound about four hundred metres across. The vent pits nearest the hall have stone sitting ledges cut into their lips, worn smooth by bodies, and in several of them cross-legged disciples sit in the heat, tiny figures with hair and clothes scorched, a few walking out of a pit, steaming, to a line of attendants with water. Above the hall a tall mast of black stone flies a long crimson banner, the loaned war banner, its cloth rippling from a hall roof. Smoke from the vents leans east on the sea wind and drifts across the whole compound. Hot gold light from the upper left, long shadows to the lower right. The vent pits are numbered by painted stones, and the nearest are linked by duckboards across the scorched ground. The hall's lowest tier holds a bath-house of black stone, where disciples cool off in tanks of spring water brought by a clay pipe from far off. The levy's barracks is a long low block with two hundred bunks, and the forge makes cooking pots and armour. A mast of black stone, thirty metres tall, stands on the highest tier; the loaned crimson banner on it is split at one edge.

places.name: Ngũ Thải Thành
places.size: A walled port city on a river mouth: about 3 km across, some 25,000 roofs and 110,000 people, in five coloured wards, with a harbour.
places.where: Grassland at sea level, river and coast, warm southern coast. Water qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung since 590, built 300 by Xích Thành Môn. Nearest: the spirit vein Thải Vũ Mạch 90 km, the lightning wood Lôi Ngô Lâm 177 km. Map crop: a river mouth at the north tip of a headland, with bare grey rocky mountains to the west and south-west, a green forested ridge beyond and the sea to the north and east; the city's coast faces open water.
places.imagined: From the hills at sunset, the city like a bird's spread wing in five colours.
places.subject: The place: Ngũ Thải Thành, Five-Colour City, seen from above and from the hills toward the sea. Setting: a warm southern coast with a wide river entering a bright blue-green gulf, green lowlands with banana and rice fields, red cliffs far off. The city is a walled port about three kilometres across with a pale stone wall and a harbour, laid out in five wards radiating from a central market square, each roofed in glazed tile of one colour: red, yellow, green, white and black, in dense blocks of roofs, about twenty-five thousand in all, so that from above the city looks like a bird's spread wing in five bands of colour, with feather-like lines of streets and canals running between. Each ward has its guild hall with a larger roof of the same colour, and quarrelling wards have markings of repaired roofs bright against old ones. A gate tower painted with a five-coloured bird faces the harbour, a grand arch of red pillars with a bird with a long tail in red, yellow, green, white and black. The harbour basin holds seventy ships with coloured sails; quays and warehouses line the water. Tiny crowds fill the squares and quays. Warm gold light from the upper left, long shadows. The five wards are laid out as a fan: the red ward in the south, the yellow in the east, the green in the north, the white in the west and the black at the centre by the harbour. Their glazed tiles are made by guild kilns on the hills, and each year's repairs are marked by a brighter patch. The gate tower's bird has a spread tail of coloured enamel, twelve metres wide. The market square is a mosaic of the five colours, and on festival days the five guilds march behind poles with a feather of their own colour. Dye-works along the river stain the water in five bands.

places.name: Thạch Cơ Thành
places.size: A walled harbour city built around a long stone jetty about 1.5 km long: city about 2.2 km across, some 14,000 roofs and 60,000 people.
places.where: Flat grassland at sea level on the coast. Earth qi. Holder Phượng Minh Cung; rose in 776 around the jetty where fleets gathered for the Pirate Purge. Nearest: the spirit vein Bàn Thạch Huyệt 127 km, the village Tử Thái 177 km. Map crop: a narrow blue gulf inlet reaching north between golden rolling hills, with paddy plots and braided river channels in the north-west, forest pockets in the south-east, and the open sea at the left edge; the city is on the inlet's eastern shore.
places.imagined: A long grey jetty reaching out into the gulf, its outer end rebuilt in bright red stone.
places.subject: The place: Thạch Cơ Thành, Stone Jetty City, seen from above a flat stretch of coast. Setting: golden rolling hills with paddy plots in the north meeting a narrow blue gulf inlet, the city on its eastern shore, low surf, a few small islands offshore, wide pale sky. The city is a walled harbour about two kilometres across with a grey stone wall and gate towers on the land side, laid out around a long stone jetty that juts far out into the gulf, about a kilometre and a half long and thirty metres wide, with a broad paved top. About fourteen thousand grey-tile roofs lie in dense blocks on either side of the jetty root, with a market square, warehouses along the quays on both sides of the jetty, shipyards, and two harbour basins sheltered by the jetty holding about sixty ships. Most of the jetty is grey, sea-worn stone, but its outer end has been rebuilt in bright red stone that stands out against the water, a quarter of its length, with a red-roofed lighthouse tower at its tip. Crowds of porters, carts and sailors move on the jetty, tiny figures, and a pair of old sailors mutter by the red joint. Light from the upper left, long shadows, sparkling sea. The jetty's grey section is made of huge square blocks, each two metres long, and the red section of stone that glows a rosy brick colour in the sun. The red lighthouse tower has a lantern room with a lamp of oiled wick. Two harbour basins on either side of the jetty root are crowded with fishing boats and traders, and shipwrights' yards ring with hammers. A row of six old stone bollards, each carved with a ship, runs along the jetty's edge. Old sailors sit on the jetty at the red joint on stools, repairing nets and shaking their heads.

places.size: A walled coastal silk town of about 1,300 roofs and 6,000 people, surrounded by about 300 hectares of mulberry rows and about 60 silkworm sheds.

places.subject: The place: Tang Điền Trấn, Mulberry Field Town, seen from above rust-red coastal land. Setting: rust-red and gold earth on the north shore of a blue bay, a huge grey-brown volcanic cone rising just south-east of the town with dark forest on its flanks, and a long cart road along the shore. The town is walled, about seven hundred metres across, with a pale stone wall, four gates, about thirteen hundred grey-tile roofs, a market square, reeling houses with tall chimneys sending up steam, dyers' yards with vats and cloth drying in long coloured lines, and a small harbour. Surrounding it, long rows of mulberry bushes cover about three hundred hectares in neat dark-green stripes on the red soil, hundreds of rows, with narrow lanes between. Among the rows stand about sixty low two-storey silkworm sheds with slatted wooden walls, long and pale, in lines, with leaf-carriers streaming between them with baskets of mulberry leaves, and in season the whole town is wreathed in steam from boiling cocoons. Silk women in headscarves, a few hundred tiny figures, pick leaves in the rows and carry baskets of cocoons. Ox-carts piled with bales of silk wait at the gate. Warm light from the upper left, long shadows across the red earth. The mulberry rows run in long curves following the contours of the red slope, each bush pruned to the height of a woman's waist, and the silkworm sheds stand at the end of every tenth row. In the reeling houses, women stir cocoons in steaming copper vats and draw the thread onto great wooden reels. The red soil stains every cart wheel and every pair of sandals. A small shrine to the silkworm goddess stands at the main gate, with a basket of fresh leaves offered at its foot. Smoke from the nearby volcano drifts across the fields on windy days.
